name: Torso-to-legs ratio

lead: Torso-to-legs ratio compares trunk length with leg length. People discuss it because longer legs relative to the body tend to read as a taller, leaner frame, and a lot of fashion advice is built on visually lengthening the legs.

There is no single accepted definition of leg length: the most common measure is perineum to floor, and a sitting-height ratio is another method. Studies of attractiveness have found preferences vary by sex and rater.

paras: People measure sitting height against standing height, then use clothing to change the look: high-rise trousers, tonal outfits, shoes that continue the leg line, and tops tailored to avoid cutting the body in half. Some use lifts to add leg height.
The proportion itself is not modifiable after growth in any routine way. Limb-lengthening surgery is a separate and high-risk topic. Fixation on proportions can distort how people see themselves.

chain: Use clothing and shoes to lengthen the leg line
angle.text: Proportion affects perceived height and balance. People adjust the look with high-rise cuts, matching colours and lifts, since the underlying skeleton is fixed.

lead: Torso-to-legs ratio is the relationship between the length of the trunk and the length of the legs. In looksmaxxing and fashion discussion, relatively long legs are associated with a taller, more athletic silhouette, and people use styling to change how the proportion looks.

Leg length has no single definition. The most common measure is perineum to floor; ankle-bone-to-outer-hip distance is arguably more rigorous, and a sitting-body ratio uses seated trunk height with leg length derived from standing height [1]. In art, legs are typically about 3.5 to 4 head-heights long [1].

Studies report preferences vary: a 2018 study cited on Wikipedia found American women rated a 1:2 leg-to-body ratio as most attractive in men, while a Japanese study found women with legs longer than their body were rated more attractive [1].
infobox: Perineum-to-floor leg length; sitting height ratio [1]

paras: Because definitions differ, studies use measures like knee height from the patella with the knee flexed at 90 degrees, which has been used to estimate adult stature [2]. Growth charts for children use sitting height and leg length to monitor proportion.

In short-statured children, trunk-to-leg ratio does not seem to depend on growth hormone sufficiency and is not changed by growth hormone treatment, according to a review of skeletal dysplasias and short stature [3].

Wikipedia notes that fashion and decorative art often show elongated limbs, while comic figures are drawn with short limbs [1]. Large deviations from the average leg-to-body ratio were noted in a Japanese study as associated with disease [1].

Research relevant to proportion includes anthropometric studies such as lower-leg-length stature equations [2] and the growth-hormone review above [3]. No studies found on interventions that change torso-to-leg ratio for appearance.
